title: Dance crowds, popular tunes, day jobs, and meeting his wife
summary: He recalls nightly dances falling off with nightclubs, well-behaved crowds, spirituals and improvising, popular tunes like High Society, band members' day jobs, Bunk as a bachelor, and how his wife inspired him to learn music.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Almost every night of the week or just the weekend? At that time we were playing every night. Oh my. I guess people really like to dance a lot more than they do now. After they start to be nightclubs, the dances start to fall off. Well that's a surprising statement to make, isn't it? I wonder why. Generally speaking, were the people who attended the dances at this time pretty well behaved Mr. Fontenet? Most of them were. You didn't have to have a floor walk in those? Well, one of two places it was, but most of the places. Everyone just came and enjoyed themselves and danced. There was one man in New York City named Grossman talking about jazz. He felt that there was a big religious influence in that. Do you feel that that is true? I feel that this is something. Can you tell us exactly why you feel that? Is it because you used spirituals in your combinations at any time? Well, the reason I said that during that time playing jazz, especially if you were improvising, you would have to have a lot of people. It's a kind of feeling that you would have. Emotional. That's it. That's it. Can you recall the names of some of the most popular pieces that your group played during the years that come to mind? Do any of them come to mind? Well, during that time, Blackball was one of the numbers. Blackball. Blackball is the one. Peace out. Our name was Smiles. Uh-huh. Now those were popular tunes? Yeah, they were popular tunes. They were popular tunes. Did you play any of the Dixieland tunes also at that time, the High Society or whatever? High Society was one of the popular numbers, was it? Very popular. In fact, it's still popular. Yes, that's right. Was there any special music, let's say, that from New Orleans your group played? Were there any compositions that were popular down there? Well, High Society was one. That's originally in New Orleans. That's right. Did your group ever play in New Orleans or visit down there at any time? With Manor Man? We never played. We had called on two occasions. We were engaged. We couldn't take the job. But I used to visit New Orleans frequently. You knew some of the players down there? Most of the whole. I'd like to ask you this. What did most of the men do in your band and in the band that you know in this area? In what spare time they had, were they particularly interested in anything outside of their music or did they spend most of their time on the music itself? Well, in our, Ed Reedum, he was a carpenter. Adam Broussard was a barber and I was. We had very little time. We had to have someone in the place all the time. Well, just about everyone worked during the day and they played at night. We couldn't do it. We just went to Raglan. We had to have somebody there. We had to work your business for you. We were among you. Sometimes we would leave and deal with it for four days, four or five days. Oh, is that right? Oh. And you had to get someone there to supply for you in your shop. Did most of the men get married that you mentioned being among your group here or were most of them all bachelors? What did most of them? I don't know. They were married. Bunk was about the biggest bachelor. Bunk Johnson? Yeah. He married late on, but everybody else were married. That's difficult. Just going to New Orleans to visit. I met my wife. I didn't meet my wife to me. That's why I became interested in music. One night we went out there dancing. And I don't remember just what band was playing. Thought comes to me that I want to learn to play dance. That's when you were around. How old were you then? Well, I guess I was about sixteen years old. And you started when you were seven or seven. And when did you get married? I was twenty-one years old. Uh-huh. Was your wife interested in music too, Mr. Funday? No. She wasn't interested in music, but she liked to sing. Uh-huh. And that had a good deal to do with helping me to improvise.
